cards.front: microorganism
cards.back: A living thing so small you need a microscope to see it. Bacteria, viruses and some fungi are examples.
cards.say: microorganism. A living thing so small you need a microscope to see it. Bacteria, viruses and some fungi are examples.

cards.front: germ
cards.back: A microorganism that can cause disease.
cards.say: germ. A microorganism that can cause disease.

cards.front: bacteria
cards.back: Tiny living cells. Some cause illness, such as food poisoning, but many are helpful.
cards.say: bacteria. Tiny living cells. Some cause illness, such as food poisoning, but many are helpful.

cards.front: virus
cards.back: A germ even smaller than bacteria. Colds, flu and measles are caused by viruses.
cards.say: virus. A germ even smaller than bacteria. Colds, flu and measles are caused by viruses.

cards.front: infection
cards.back: When germs get into the body and multiply, making you ill.
cards.say: infection. When germs get into the body and multiply, making you ill.

cards.front: How can germs spread through the air?
cards.back: When people cough or sneeze, tiny droplets carry germs that others may breathe in.
cards.say: How can germs spread through the air? When people cough or sneeze, tiny droplets carry germs that others may breathe in.

cards.front: How can germs spread by touch?
cards.back: Germs on hands or objects pass to other people when they touch their eyes, nose or mouth.
cards.say: How can germs spread by touch? Germs on hands or objects pass to other people when they touch their eyes, nose or mouth.

cards.front: How can germs spread in food and water?
cards.back: Dirty hands, flies and unclean water can carry germs into food and drink.
cards.say: How can germs spread in food and water? Dirty hands, flies and unclean water can carry germs into food and drink.

cards.front: vector
cards.back: An animal that carries germs from one living thing to another. Mosquitoes carry the germs that cause dengue and malaria.
cards.say: vector. An animal that carries germs from one living thing to another. Mosquitoes carry the germs that cause dengue and malaria.

cards.front: How can you reduce the spread of mosquito diseases?
cards.back: Remove standing water where mosquitoes breed, use nets and repellent.
cards.say: How can you reduce the spread of mosquito diseases? Remove standing water where mosquitoes breed, use nets and repellent.

cards.front: How long should you wash your hands to remove germs?
cards.back: At least 20 seconds, with soap and water.
cards.say: How long should you wash your hands to remove germs? At least 20 seconds, with soap and water.

cards.front: Why should you cough into your elbow?
cards.back: It catches the droplets so they do not spread to people or onto your hands.
cards.say: Why should you cough into your elbow? It catches the droplets so they do not spread to people or onto your hands.

cards.front: What are the body's first defences against germs?
cards.back: Skin, which is a barrier, and mucus in the nose that traps germs. Stomach acid kills many that are swallowed.
cards.say: What are the body's first defences against germs? Skin, which is a barrier, and mucus in the nose that traps germs. Stomach acid kills many that are swallowed.

cards.front: white blood cells
cards.back: Blood cells that find and destroy germs.
cards.say: white blood cells. Blood cells that find and destroy germs.

cards.front: antibodies
cards.back: Chemicals made by white blood cells that stick to germs and help destroy them.
cards.say: antibodies. Chemicals made by white blood cells that stick to germs and help destroy them.

cards.front: fever
cards.back: A higher body temperature than normal. It helps the body to fight an infection.
cards.say: fever. A higher body temperature than normal. It helps the body to fight an infection.

cards.front: vaccine
cards.back: A medicine, often an injection, that prepares the body to fight a particular germ.
cards.say: vaccine. A medicine, often an injection, that prepares the body to fight a particular germ.

cards.front: How does a vaccine protect you?
cards.back: It teaches the body to make antibodies, so it can fight the real germ quickly.
cards.say: How does a vaccine protect you? It teaches the body to make antibodies, so it can fight the real germ quickly.

cards.front: immune
cards.back: Protected against a disease.
cards.say: immune. Protected against a disease.

cards.front: antibiotic
cards.back: A medicine that kills bacteria. It does not work on viruses.
cards.say: antibiotic. A medicine that kills bacteria. It does not work on viruses.

cards.front: Will an antibiotic cure a cold?
cards.back: No. A cold is caused by a virus, and antibiotics only work on bacteria.
cards.say: Will an antibiotic cure a cold? No. A cold is caused by a virus, and antibiotics only work on bacteria.

cards.front: Why is food kept in a fridge?
cards.back: The cold slows the growth of bacteria, so food stays fresh longer.
cards.say: Why is food kept in a fridge? The cold slows the growth of bacteria, so food stays fresh longer.

cards.front: Why should you stay at home when you have an infectious illness?
cards.back: So that you do not spread germs to other people.
cards.say: Why should you stay at home when you have an infectious illness? So that you do not spread germs to other people.

cards.front: Who discovered penicillin, the first antibiotic?
cards.back: Alexander Fleming, in 1928.
cards.say: Who discovered penicillin, the first antibiotic? Alexander Fleming, in 1928.
